lead: A beam carries shear force as well as bending moment. The shear force does not spread evenly over the section: it produces a shear stress τ that changes with height, found from τ = VQ/(Ib). The same idea gives shear flow q = VQ/I along a joint. Engineers use it to check webs of steel beams, to space bolts and welds in built-up sections, and to avoid shear failure near supports where V is largest.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for centroid and second moment of area, and Unit 3 for shear force diagrams.

blocks.text: A shear force V on a section is not spread evenly as V/A. It creates a shear stress τ that changes with height. The formula is τ = VQ/(Ib).

blocks.where: τ is shear stress at a chosen level, in N/mm² (same as MPa); V is shear force at the section, in N; Q is first moment about the neutral axis of the area beyond that level, in mm³; I is second moment of area of the whole section about the neutral axis, in mm⁴; b is width of the section at that level, in mm; q is shear flow, in N/mm.

blocks.text: Q = A1 × y1. A1 is the area beyond the level, and y1 is the distance from its centroid to the neutral axis. Take the area above or below the level; both give the same Q. At a free top or bottom surface the area beyond is zero, so τ = 0. At the neutral axis Q is largest for a rectangle, so τ is largest there.

The vertical shear stress has an equal horizontal shear stress on a small element. That is why the same formula gives the shear between flange and web, or between a beam and a bolted plate. Some syllabi call it horizontal shear stress. Use the level where you want the stress, not a fixed level.

For a rectangle of width b and depth d, I = bd³/12 and A = bd. At height y from the neutral axis, τ = V/(2I)(d²/4 − y²). At y = 0, τ_max = 1.5 V/A. At y = ±d/2, τ = 0. For a solid circle of diameter d, τ_max = 4/3 V/A at the centre. For a triangle, the maximum is 1.5 V/A at mid-height; its neutral axis is at h/3 from the base.
These factors are not the average. V/A is the average shear stress. For a rectangle the peak is half as large again. A common exam error is to answer V/A as the maximum.

For a symmetric hollow circle or box, the peak is at the centre. Use b as the total material width at that level: 2(R − r) for a hollow circle, where R is the outer radius and r is the inner radius, and twice the wall thickness at a web level for a box. For unsymmetrical sections, compute Q and b at each level to locate the peak.

sections.h3: I- and T-sections: the web carries most shear

blocks.text: In an I- or T-section, almost all shear force is carried by the web. The flanges are thin and far from the neutral axis; the web is the continuous vertical plate. At a level in the web, b is the web thickness t_w. At a level in a flange, b is the full flange width. So τ drops sharply when the level crosses from web into flange.

To find τ at a level, use Q of the area above that level. In the web, that area includes the top flange plus the part of the web above the level. At the neutral axis, Q is largest and b = t_w, so τ is usually largest there.

items: Locate the neutral axis and find I for the whole section.
Choose the level y where τ is needed.
Find the area beyond y and its centroid distance y1 from the neutral axis.
Take b as the width at that level.
Use τ = VQ/(Ib). For shear flow use q = VQ/I.

blocks.text: Shear flow q is useful for bolts and welds. A weld joining flange to web must supply q N per mm of beam length. If the weld strength is s N per mm of weld length and a length L mm of weld is laid in each pitch p, then sL/p ≥ q, so p ≤ sL/q. Equivalently, the required weld length per unit beam length is q/s.

figure.caption: Shear stress at each height for the 200 mm deep rectangular beam of the worked example. The stress is zero at the top and bottom fibres and reaches 4.5 MPa at the neutral axis.

examples.question: A rectangular beam 100 mm wide and 200 mm deep carries a shear force of 60 kN. Find the maximum shear stress and the shear stress at 50 mm from the neutral axis.
steps: At y = 50 mm, area above the level = 100 × 50 = 5,000 mm². Its centroid is 75 mm from the neutral axis, so Q = 5,000 × 75 = 375,000 mm³.
examples.answer: I = 66,666,666.7 mm⁴, A = 20,000 mm², maximum shear stress = 4.5 MPa at the neutral axis, and shear stress at 50 mm from the neutral axis = 3.375 MPa.
examples.check:
V = 60000.0
b = 100.0
d = 200.0
I = b * d**3 / 12
A = b * d
tau_max = 1.5 * V / A
y = 50.0
tau_y = V / (2 * I) * ((d/2)**2 - y**2)
print(round(I, 1))
print(round(A, 1))
print(tau_max)
print(tau_y)

traps: Using V/A as the maximum shear stress. For a rectangle the peak is 1.5 V/A, for a solid circle 4/3 V/A.
In an I-section, taking b as flange width at the neutral axis. At the neutral axis b is the web thickness.
Using the area itself as Q. Q is area times the distance from its centroid to the neutral axis, so Q has units of mm³.
Mixing metres and millimetres. Use N and mm throughout to get N/mm², which is MPa.
Forgetting that b changes at a flange-web junction. The shear stress jumps there; the web value is the one that matters for shear design.

quiz.q: State the shear stress formula for a beam section and define each symbol.
quiz.a: τ = VQ/(Ib): V is shear force, Q is first moment of the area beyond the level about the neutral axis, I is second moment of area of the whole section, b is width at the level.

quiz.q: Why is shear stress zero at the top and bottom fibres of a rectangle, and maximum at the neutral axis?
quiz.a: At a free surface the area beyond the level is zero, so Q = 0 and τ = 0. At the neutral axis Q is largest for a rectangle, and b is constant, so τ is largest.

quiz.q: A rectangular beam 80 mm wide and 160 mm deep carries a shear force of 40 kN. Find the maximum shear stress.
In an I-section, why is the shear stress much larger in the web than in the flange at the same shear force?
quiz.a: The web is narrow, so b is small. It is also near the neutral axis where Q is large. The flange is wide, so b is large and τ is small.

quiz.q: A solid circular shaft of diameter 120 mm carries a shear force of 50 kN. Find the maximum shear stress.
What is shear flow q, and what are its units?
quiz.a: q = VQ/I is shear force per unit length along a joint. Its units are N/mm. It is used to space bolts or welds.

quiz.q: At the junction of flange and web in an I-section, which value of b should be used to check shear stress in the web?
quiz.a: Use the web thickness t_w just below the junction. The flange width applies inside the flange, where shear stress is small. The web carries most shear.

beyond: Not for the exam. Shear flow q = VQ/I sizes welds and bolts in built-up girders, castellated beams and aircraft stringers. Finite element codes report shear stress components, and the same VQ/(Ib) idea is checked against von Mises stress. Search for shear flow in built-up sections, shear lag in wide flanges, and shear connectors in composite beams.
